DACF is fi.1lly committed to supporting robust meat processing infrastructure and an adequate workforce to meet the demands of Maine farmers and food producers. We have, for example,
supported the industry with material resources. In the last five years, we have channeled an
unprecedented $40 million in infrastructure investments into food and agriculture businesses in Maine, with $6.3 million, or about 16%, going to meat and poultry processors.
We have also demonstrated a willingness to respond to the needs of meat processing businesses. We heard the complaint that sudden, unexpected closures, such as those associated with extreme

administrative change that accomplished that.

the inspectors' small, two-wheel-drive State vehicles for four-wheel-drive SUVs. That change cost the Department $49,000 in the first year alone. There is no appropriation from the State or
reimbursement mechanism with our federal partners to recoup that $49,000, so we have reallocated money from other Department priorities.
LD 3 ll now aims to make inspection services available on holidays and "bonus" holidays.

Good Morning Sen. Talbot-Ross, Rep. Pluecker, and members of the Joint Standing Committee
on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry. My name is Garrett Mason. I am a resident of Lisbon Falls, and am a Partner at Dirigo Public Affairs. I am here today representing our client, the
Maine Farm Bureau. We are speaking today in support of LD 311.

The Maine Farm Bureau advocates for policies that promote the viability and sustainability of our agricultural economy. LD 311 as indicated by the agricultural industry, its bipartisan cosponsorship, and the emergency preamble, is clearly a necessary and timely measure to support Maine's livestock producers, meat processors, and rural communities.

One of the most pressing challenges facing our livestock farmers is the bottleneck in meat and
poultry processing. With a limited number of USDA and state-inspected facilities, farmers often
face long wait times for slaughter and processing services. This issue was exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, which exposed vulnerabilities in our supply chain and highlighted the urgent need for more reliable and consistent processing capacity within our state.

By designating state meat and poultry inspectors as essential, LD 311 ensures that processing
facilities can continue operations without unnecessary delays. This designation would allow
inspections to continue on state holidays and beyond normal work shifts when necessary, provided that the processing establishments cover overtime costs. The bill strikes an important
balance between maintaining essential government functions while ensuring that taxpayers do
not bear additional financial burden.

Furthermore, this bill supports Maine's broader goals of strengthening our local food system.
Consumer demand for locally raised meat is growing, as more Mainers seek out sustainable,
high-quality food produced within our state. Without the processing infrastructure to meet this demand, Maine farmers are at a disadvantage. Keeping our processing facilities running efficiently benefits not only farmers but also consumers, small businesses, and rural economies.

On behalf of the Maine Farm Bureau and our Legislative Committee we would ask you to vote
ought to pass on this legislation.

Thursday, March 6, 2025

Good Morning Sen. Talbot-Ross, Rep. Pluecker, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry:

My name is Senator Stacey Guerin and I represent Senate District 4, which includes all of Piscataquis
County and ll communities in Penobscot County. I appreciate the opportunity to speak before you
today in Support of LD 31 l, "An Act to Improve Efficiency of Meat and Poultry Processing
Facilities by Requiring the Designation of State Inspectors as Essential."
This bill would make state inspections under the Maine Meat and Poultry Inspection (MMPI) program essential. As many of you know, these inspections are crucial to ensuring that our local
livestock and poultry are handled humanely, are disease-free, and are correctly labeled and packaged. Without these inspections, businesses cannot do their normal operations like slaughtering, packaging, or labeling products. This isn'tjust a small inconvenience---it has a significant ripple effect,
impacting businesses and Maine citizens who rely on locally grown food. Unfortunately, since state inspectors are not classified as essential state workers, when the state closes, these businesses and
their employees must all but halt their work.
I am before you today supporting this legislation because constituents of mine, and likely some of
yours, have been significantly impacted by these closures. Meanwhile, similar facilities that are
inspected by the U S Department of Agriculture (USDA) do not experience the same unfortunate
outcomes because their inspectors are essential. Even in cases of federal government shutdowns,
USDA inspectors continue with business as usual. This legislation would make inspections under the MMPI and licensing program essential services so when a state of emergency is declared the
facilities that fall under these programs do not suffer financial hardship and backlogs in their work.

The bill also directs the Commissioner of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry to require, rather than just authorize as current law allows, that inspections continue at these establishments on state holidays or beyond regular work shifts or workweeks, as long as the necessary inspectors are available. The business would be responsible for covering all overtime salaries for the inspections necessary to keep the plant open, as well as any other expenses caused by the overtime work. This provision is essential in making sure that these businesses can continue operating even when the normal schedule is disrupted.
By passing this bill, we can create a more level playing field for all of Maine's meat and poultry facilities. It ensures that Maine businesses aren't left struggling when state offices are closed, and it
helps guarantee that Maine citizens continue to have access to locally grown and processed food. It's a win for local businesses, workers, and consumers alike.

Thank you for your time and consideration. I urge you to support this important bill.
